393 files. Where would you look?

A Greenwood bug report says that styles and scripts go missing from server-rendered pages. The repository has 393 files to choose from. We want a short reading list—not a tour of all 393.

Watch the files line up. Qwen compares their text with the issue. Atlas adds connections between them. Jev judges the first 32, and a small rule moves its choices toward the front.

393 files → 32 judgments → 10 shown

One mark per actual file · ranks move; file identity stays fixed

Those are real files and recorded ranks. The shared helper, resource-utils.js, starts in 28th place and finishes tenth. No model is running here; the animation replays a saved result. Finding likely files is called localization.

How do “missing styles” and “resource utils” meet?

Matching words helps when the issue uses the same names as the code. But people describe symptoms, and files often name mechanisms.

Qwen is the model we use to turn text into lists of numbers, called embeddings or vectors. We obtain one list for the issue and one for each file. Similar directions in those lists can bring differently worded texts together. That is a learned clue, not proof that the file needs changing.

Once we have the numbers, sorting files is ordinary arithmetic. This is the actual Flix comparison:

dot multiplies numbers in matching positions and adds them up. norm measures each list’s length. Dividing by both lengths compares direction rather than size. The if handles an all-zero list. This score is called cosine similarity; it needs no further model call.

The first 32 files go to judgment. That is a spending limit, not a confidence threshold. File 33 could matter too. All 393 remain in the full ranking.

Ask the model once. Keep the numbers.

A new issue needs its own vector. Unchanged source files can keep theirs. In the retained acquisition, 27,733 requested rows shared 10,555 distinct embedding inputs. The cold run recorded $0.1409903 in provider charges; its replay made zero provider requests. Loading and comparing saved numbers still takes time.

Watch the requests—and the replay that avoids them →

Does the short list help?

Across 85 historical issues, Qwen puts a required file in its first ten 73 times. Jev with structural clues raises that to 78/85. Finding every required file is harder: 47/85. The difference matters when a fix touches eight files and we find only one.

The larger Sol agent comparison takes a different route: it searches and reads the repository itself. Jev’s prepared question has a 78× shorter median measured wait, and known model spend including cold Qwen acquisition is 28× smaller than Sol’s API-price estimate. These compare different amounts of work; preparation is outside Jev’s request timer. The benchmark puts the scores, costs and limitations together.

We like this division of labor: use a model for the part that benefits from one; keep the rest small enough to inspect. Next, look at the connections we can read straight from code.

effects:
Historical localization benchmark · 85 eligible issues / 22 repositories

Ask for the numbers. Wait for an answer.

A calculation needs an embedding: a list of numbers describing some text. Perhaps those numbers are saved already. Perhaps another computer must produce them. The calculation asks; something else supplies the answer; the calculation continues.

Ask. Answer. Carry on.

Executed teaching example · replay, not a measured wait

That little handoff is the idea behind a Flix effect. The request says what is needed. A handler answers it. Here the answer is already available, so the handler can hand it straight back. Nothing goes over the network.

Here is the request

This small teaching program is compiled and tested. eff introduces a request named vector: give it text, receive a list of numbers.

vectorForIssue asks for the issue’s numbers. The \ Embedding in its type tells Flix that it needs this effect. A caller cannot quietly pretend the request never happens: the compiler tracks that need through the program.

Here is the answer

run starts the calculation. When it asks for a vector, this handler receives the request and a function called continueWith. Give that function the saved numbers, and the waiting calculation resumes.

The test supplies two illustrative numbers and checks they come back unchanged. They are not Qwen measurements. Another handler could fetch an answer over the network; that handler would have to declare its own outside work too.

This is handy for testing. The calculation can ask the same question while a test supplies the answer cheaply. The Flix effect-system guide explains the compiler’s checks. Effects expose work; they do not make it free, cached or parallel.

Where did the study call Qwen?

In Java, through a hosted-model SDK. The helper saved vectors; Flix read them and ranked files. That acquisition code is preserved in the complete study snapshot. The example above supplies authored answers.

Separate inference from arithmetic

External work produces reusable data

In one recorded Greenwood run, 393 source files and one issue became 352 distinct embedding inputs. Eleven hosted requests, plus local acquisition and writing, took about 92 seconds. Once those numbers were saved, ranking needed no more inference.

See the archived Flix file boundary

FileRead.read(path) requests the saved contents; runWithIO performs that read. \ IO tells us this function touches the outside world. Result.getWithDefault returns an empty string on a read error. This wrapper reads a file; it does not call Qwen.

A new issue does not erase the old work

Change the issue below. The file vectors stay; the issue vector and ranking need new work. Change the embedding recipe instead, and the old vectors no longer answer the same request.

Change an input. See what must run again.

Highlighted boundary = affected work · no timing implied

Bazel, the build system, tracks which steps depend on which inputs. It can reuse a completed step when its declared inputs and execution identity still match. For ranking, those include the issue vector, source-file vectors and candidate list. Effects do not declare those dependencies for Bazel; the build rule does.

Saved vectors also record their model, recipe and exact input bytes. That is how we distinguish “we have this answer” from “we have some similar numbers.” A changed source file needs a new vector if its embedded input changes.

There are two useful Flix ideas here. Effects let a program say “I need an answer from outside.” Datalog lets it ask “what follows from the facts I already have?” Watch two imports produce a Datalog answer, or see how much repeated work we avoided.

Run the idea

In the current Attune checkout, run:

nix run

The offline walkthrough asks for vectors, supplies saved answers, and ranks two files. Start with Main.flix, then Effects.flix. A missing answer stops the calculation. The vectors are authored examples; no model is called.

nix run .#test checks the implementation. Flix describes requests and computes answers. Bazel schedules independent actions and reuses unchanged outputs.

Turn a line of code into a row.

Greenwood’s bundling code imports a helper. A person can read that line and point to the file it uses. We want to keep the same observation in a form a program can ask questions about.

A line of code becomes a fact

Source syntax → resolved target → admitted relationship

Grit recognizes the import’s source-code shape and captures the written name. Flix finds the actual target file and saves the relationship. The solid arrow means that target was accepted in this saved repository version.

Find this shape, whatever the names are

Here is the actual Grit pattern:

The backticks describe source syntax. $source is a blank Grit fills with the module name; as $import captures the whole statement. or allows either shape. log records the match. It does not decide which file the name means.

In this case the captured text is '../lib/resource-utils.js'. The .. says to go up one folder from lifecycles/bundle.js, then into lib. Now we can check whether that target exists.

Keep only the connections we can justify

source text
  |
Grit: find the import, capture its name
  |
Java: carry the match and its source location
  |
Flix: find the target in this repository version
  |
  +-- found ------> save the relationship
  '--- unresolved -> keep a refusal, not a guess

The same pipeline reads three kinds of facts: a file defines a named function or other code item; a file imports another file; one named item calls another. Reverse questions read those same pairs backward. Finding “is imported by” does not need a second extraction pass.

Different languages, the same columns

Ruby writes a relative require. JavaScript writes an import. Each needs its own source pattern and rules for finding targets. Once resolved, both become rows with the same columns:

Different syntax → the same relationship columns

Ruby shop fixture + retained Greenwood JavaScript · two separate worlds

The world column keeps repository versions apart. Source locations let us check where a row came from. Downstream code can ask “which files share this dependency?” without learning Ruby or JavaScript syntax again. That is where Datalog comes in.

Sometimes the spelling defeats the reader

Got imports response.js, but the retained file is response.ts. The source resolver tries the given name and appends possible endings. It does not replace .js with .ts. So this real dependency never becomes an accepted Imports row.

A real dependency, a missing fact

Dotted arrow = source-confirmed, not admitted by Atlas

The dots mean present in source, absent from Atlas’s facts. Qwen and Jev still find both required files. Missing a connection limits the questions Atlas can answer; it does not make the file invisible to every method.

The exact rule that misses the .js → .ts connection

base is the normalized source name. List.map appends each suffix to it. :: puts one item at the front of a list; ::: joins lists. None of these operations replaces an existing extension.

The native Grit matcher also records byte ranges—the positions of the matched text. Java carries these records into Flix, which checks source identity and resolves the target. The shared table format does not remove this language-specific work. The JavaScript pattern also understands JSX, JavaScript’s embedded markup syntax.

A tiny answer can take a long time

Now watch the recorded build. Each row is one repository version. Amber marks a running extraction process; the thin grey line shows the longer lifetime of its scheduled build step.

Watch the build unfold

Horizontal position = recorded minutes · one row per world

There are 92 extraction actions, with process timings for 90. The median process takes 93.8 seconds: half finish faster, half slower. The mean is 344.6 seconds. A few stragglers pull it up; the longest takes 42.5 minutes, about 27× the median.

The average hides a long tail

90 recorded processes · one dot each · two views of the same durations

The box holds the middle half, 62.6–279.8 seconds. The eleven points beyond the upper whisker come from just four repository groups: FHIR/Sushi, ESLint, Obsidian Tasks and Carbon. Repeated versions are not independent repository families. The two slowest completed intervals are Obsidian Tasks, at 42.0 and 42.5 minutes.

This timer covers Grit, Java transport and Flix checks and resolution together. We cannot honestly call all of it parsing. Theory, the later step that asks questions of the facts, has a separate 20.6-second median over ninety process intervals.

One smaller diagnostic did isolate a parser problem: a 325 KB TypeScript test file took 360.6 seconds, yielded no accepted definitions, imports or calls, and produced 4,106 refusals. That case in the localization report is attributed to the pinned native parser. Small output, very large wait.

What this timing record includes—and cannot tell us

The build was partly cached and interrupted. It lasted 18,118.178 seconds and predates the exclusions that leave 85 eligible issues. Worlds w41 and w84 have no process interval; they are unknown, not zero. The distribution excludes those two missing observations.

An action’s lifetime includes more than its process interval. We cannot split the remaining time reliably into queueing, transfer and orchestration, or split the process into its internal stages. Adding overlapping intervals measures work, not elapsed wall time. “Outlier” means exceeding the chart’s statistical cutoff; it does not by itself identify a parser bug.

Saving this work matters. A later Attune checkpoint reused extraction for 158 files and read only five afresh. Wall Time shows that reuse. Once the facts exist, Atlas can ask its small questions.

Follow the files through the ranking

Up = a better rank · dashed line = top-ten cutoff

A rank is a place in the list, not a probability. Moving up helps only if we are moving the right files. These are recorded results: replay shows their saved positions, not a model thinking.

What does Jev actually do?

Jev is the model judging Qwen’s first 32 files. It receives the issue and a short record for each candidate, then answers Relevant, NotRelevant or Unknown. Flix puts the Relevant group first and keeps Qwen’s order inside each group.

Relevant gets group 0; the others get group 1. The second part of the sorting key is the original Qwen rank. Nobody is deleted. Even an unchanged judgment can move down when other files move ahead of it. Unknown and failed observations do not receive promotion, but they are not negative judgments.

What difference does the extra note make?

One starting list. Two separate judgments.

QJ and QS both begin with the original Qwen ranking

QJ and QS are alternatives over the same original Qwen list. QJ gives Jev the issue, paths, original ranks and similarity scores. QS adds Atlas’s note: what a file defines, imports and is imported by, plus IDs of saved structural answers associated with its definitions.

That note contains counts, up to six names per relationship family and up to eight distinct answer IDs. It contains neither source bodies nor a graph-navigation tool. A file below Qwen’s first 32 is not judged, even if a note happens to mention it.

The two calls use the same starting list

Both calls use q. The separate lists dq and dqs hold basic and structural decisions. The historical fix is checked afterward; it is not supplied to the judge.

Something is much easier than everything

On 85 issues, Qwen finds at least one required file in its first ten 73 times. Jev raises that to 77. With structural clues, 78. But that last condition finds every required file only 47 times.

One ranking. Two definitions of success.

One mark per issue · # recovered · . incomplete or missed

Among the 44 multi-file issues, QS finds something 41 times and everything ten times. The gaps are actual unfinished localizations, even when the top answer looks excellent. The benchmark compares every method and explains the scores.

Paired QJ / QS outcomes · all 85 eligible tasks · top ten

No issue loses its binary top-ten success in that paired comparison. Individual files still get worse, as Obsidian shows. A score that asks only “did we find anything?” can hide a lot.

Greenwood shows a helpful change: the helper’s answer becomes Relevant and all eight fixing files enter the top ten. Got shows a missing Atlas import even though retrieval finds both fixing files. The records below keep those cases beside the Obsidian regression.

Can we find two files using the same helper?

Receipt and checkout both import pricing in a small, checked Ruby shop example. Look for the repeated name:

Two facts. Two different consumers.

Ruby shop fixture · an explanatory replay of a checked query

We keep two known imports as facts. Then write a rule saying that two different files form a pair when they import the same target. That is Datalog: rules that combine known facts to answer questions.

Here is the rule from the original shop example. Its source and tests are preserved here; the current README shows a shorter version of the same question:

Read :- as “if.” A Pair exists if both Imports lines match. The repeated center makes the target identical in both; a != b keeps a file from pairing with itself. Repeating s keeps the observations in the same repository world.

a, b and center are blanks filled from the rows—variables. Connecting rows through the same blank is a join. No filename is hardcoded in the rule.

Ask many little questions

Inspect the machine: six relationships, real Theory code and saved rows

The common vocabulary

A file is a source path. A symbol is a named definition, such as a function. Grit extracts definitions, imports and calls. Flix admits justified targets, then reverses those same pairs to provide three backward directions. They are not six independent measurements.

Three observations. Six directions.

Solid arrows = admitted relationships · reverse arrows read the same facts

Different syntax → the same relationship columns

Ruby shop fixture + retained Greenwood JavaScript · two separate worlds

Starting from a symbol, DefinedIn finds its file; ImportedBy finds that file’s users. A sequence of such lookups is a route. Each operation accepts files or symbols and returns a new set of the declared type.

A symbol → its file → the importers

Greenwood w49 · three exact intermediate sets

Theory: write a small question as data

Once “who shares a dependency?” works, we can ask nearby questions: who calls a name defined here? Which file contains the thing that this function calls? Each question rearranges a few of the same relationship lookups.

Attune.Theory writes these little questions down as data. A descriptor is a recipe with three fields. atoms lists the required relationships. denied lists pairs of positions that must hold different values. outputs lists which positions to return. The evaluator can read many such recipes without generating a new source file for each one.

The supported grammar permits one to three positive two-ended relationships, up to four typed positions, one or two output positions, and an optional inequality. “Positive” means requiring a fact to exist. The relationships must connect, and every returned position must occur in a relationship. These limits make a finite, inspectable family; they do not amount to unrestricted rule generation.

The following descriptors were checked and executed through the current Theory implementation on tiny authored facts. A numbered position is just a blank to fill, like a, b or center in the shop rule. Position 0 does not mean “the first file in the repository.” It means “the first named place in this question.”

The braces hold a record: named fields grouped into one value. outputs = 0 :: 1 :: Nil says “return position 0, followed by position 1, then end the list.” :: builds a list and Nil is the empty list at its end. denied = Nil says there are no pairs required to differ. For comparison, denied = (0, 2) :: Nil would require the values at positions 0 and 2 to differ. That is the descriptor’s counterpart of a != b.

Read the diagrams first, then the comments. They describe the same small operation.

one relationship
[0: File] --Imports--> [1: File]
return 0, 1
two relationships
[0: File] --Imports--> [1: File]
[2: File] --Imports--> [1: File]
return 0, 2; they may be the same file
three relationships
[0: File] --Defines--> [1: Symbol]
[1: Symbol] --Calls--> [2: Symbol]
[2: Symbol] --DefinedIn--> [3: File]
return 0, 3

That third question asks which file defines a caller, and which file contains the thing it calls. It is legal and passes the small executable example. It was not part of the frozen 72-candidate study below. The retained template family uses only one or two relationships and no inequality.

Match the recipe against the facts

There are two tables to read. The recipe table, called Desc, says which relationships the question requires. The fact table, called Edge, says which relationships actually exist in the world. The engine must find facts that satisfy the recipe.

Take the two-import question. The recipe says: find an Imports row from position 0 to position 1, then another Imports row from position 2 to that same position 1. The actual file names fill those positions. A successful filling is called a binding—nothing more mysterious than names assigned to the blanks.

The code below is the real shared-target rule, with explanatory comments added. Instead of hardcoding Imports, it reads r0 and r1, the two relationship names, from the recipe. That lets the same checked rule handle other compatible pairs of relationships.

Binding(...) is the row we want to produce. Desc(...) reads the recipe. The two Edge(...) lines find its supporting facts. Because both repeat w and e1, they must agree on the world and shared target. The shape string chooses this arrangement of arrows: 0 → 1 and 2 → 1.

The final three lines implement the optional “these positions must be different” conditions. Each line allows a match if that pair was not constrained, or if its two values really differ. In the frozen 72-question family no inequality was requested, so these checks do not remove self-pairs.

There is one bookkeeping detail: the stored binding reserves four positions for all supported question shapes. This shape needs only three, so its last e0 is filler. It is not an additional source relationship. The underscores _ mean “this rule does not need this column.”

Once a binding exists, we still have to decide what to return. In the shared-dependency example, we might want both consumers, or only the shared target. The input facts can be identical while the requested answer differs.

The second rule reads the output positions from the recipe and selects those values:

role(out0, ...) selects one position from the match; role(out1, ...) selects the other. This is projection: returning only selected columns. Several different matches can produce the same output row, so the saved answer can be much smaller than the internal work.

A rule meets the retained rows

Choose a question · facts, bindings, saved answer and measured frequency

The first example has two importing files but returns only the shared target. They produce one saved answer, not two. For a one-column question, Theory’s fixed output format repeats that value in its two output slots. The stored row still counts once. The small rule shown in the graphic is an executed, specialized reading of the descriptor; production uses the general rule family above.

Most of these structures are ordinary

Bar length = descriptors · color = number of relation atoms

The retained matrix has 5,832 evaluated question/world pairs and 186 observed empty results. Its 1,406,061 saved output rows are distinct within each question/world pair. They are not the full number of internal matches, unique files or independent architectural examples. The frozen questions have no inequality: repeated positions can refer to the same item, so some two-connection questions detect very ordinary single-edge properties.

Reuse the expensive answer; ask a new small question

The source world and structural question determine the matched rows. The wording of a new issue does not change those rows. We can therefore keep the world’s prepared answers and select the ones useful for a new candidate, instead of repeating the full structural calculation for every issue.

Theory makes this split explicit. Output is the prepared answer table. Anchor names an item we want to focus on. This actual rule selects prepared rows whose first output matches that item:

Read it as “return this task-specific row if it is already an Output row, and its first item is an Anchor in the same world.” c keeps the question’s identity; w keeps the world’s identity. This is a lookup into answers already computed. It does not rerun the source reader or reconstruct the relationships.

The frozen Jev prompt writer performs its own bounded lookup against retained answers, using the candidate’s defined symbols. The rule above shows Theory’s explicit reuse boundary; it is not a claim that the Java writer invokes that exact Flix rule for each note.

There is also reuse inside a route. Two different sequences of lookups can reach the same exact set. If they ask the same next question in the same world and scope, that calculation can be shared. The architecture page compares this with prefix caching and shows the actual key.

These properties have three different payoffs. For localization, source connections add evidence about a candidate’s role. For wall time, retained facts and answers avoid repeating preparation, while unchanged file acquisitions can survive a source edit. For architecture, the same fixed questions produce different patterns of empty answers and repeated calculations across repositories. None of these observations alone establishes the other two. A cheaply reused empty answer can describe the graph accurately while providing no clue to a fix.

What about rules that keep going?

So far, our rules make a bounded number of lookups. Recursion means a rule can use results produced by that same relationship. Imagine a screen importing a formatter, which imports a units helper:

[screen] --Imports--> [format] --Imports--> [units]
    |                                        ^
    `--------------- Reaches ----------------'

The first rule turns direct imports into reachability. The second extends a known path by one import. Evaluation repeats until no new rows appear—a fixpoint. This separate, executed teaching example returns the two direct connections and screen → units. It is not a claim that the frozen Theory study generated recursive queries.

Datalog has costs: finding matches, storing intermediate values and updating results after changes all take work. Zhao and colleagues’ FlowLog: Efficient and Extensible Datalog via Incrementality (2025 preprint; VLDB 2026) studies another engine that reuses relational work as inputs change. It is relevant research, not Attune’s implementation or a measured Attune speedup.

Outside work, then questions about its answers

Reading files and asking a model for numbers need the outside world. Effects make those requests visible in Flix. Once we have the facts, Datalog asks questions about them. Neither automatically provides caching or scheduling; the saved identities and runtime must do that work.

The admitted candidate files are JavaScript/TypeScript-family source, including tests. Eligible gold includes supported existing source paths changed, deleted or renamed by the fix; it excludes new files and tests. All 218 eligible gold occurrences are present in their task’s candidate list. This measures finding eligible modified files, not every file a developer might need to understand the issue.

Each task has its own candidate set. Across the 85 eligible lists there are 28,370 file occurrences. The often-quoted 29,493 counts all 88 surviving task lists, including duplicated files when tasks share a world. It is not one giant search space or a count of unique files.

The frozen eligible splits contain 50 development tasks from 13 groups, 20 calibration tasks from five groups, and 15 final tasks from four groups. The all-task view is descriptive; the final split is small. The panel concentrates on web frameworks, Node tooling, linting and developer utilities. It does not establish coverage of arbitrary languages or repository families.

What does a success mean?

Slide the cutoff below. You are reading farther down the same saved ranking, not asking for a better prediction. Each # is a file in Greenwood’s historical fix.

Move the cutoff. Watch the score.

Frozen Greenwood Qwen ranking · # eligible required path · . other candidate

The @k means “look only at the first k returned paths.” A required file at rank 11 is missed at ten, even if the full ranking contains it. These measurements answer different questions:

  • Hit@k — did we find anything? One if at least one eligible required file appears; zero otherwise.
  • Complete@k — did we find everything? One only if every eligible required file appears. The canonical Flix name is FileAcc@k.
  • Recall@k — how much of the fix did we find? Recovered required files divided by that task’s required-file count.
  • MRR@k — how early was the first hit? The reciprocal of its rank: rank one gives 1, rank two gives 1/2. No hit inside k gives zero. The table’s MRR averages this over tasks.

At ten, Greenwood’s Qwen ranking contains five of eight eligible required files. That is a Hit of 1, Complete of 0, Recall of 5/8, and reciprocal rank of 1 because the first file is relevant. Expanding the window to 28 finally includes all eight. No prediction changed; only the cutoff changed.

Read the exact Flix scoring rule

The evaluator first takes the prediction prefix. Then it keeps the gold paths found in that prefix. List.memberOf is an exact path-membership check: a plausible filename or a neighboring file does not earn partial credit for that path.

Hit asks whether that recovered list is nonempty. Complete recovery compares its length with the gold list’s length. Here is the actual complete-recovery rule; not List.isEmpty(gold) prevents an empty label from becoming a vacuous success.

Ineligible tasks are excluded before aggregation. An eligible task with an abstention or a failed prediction stays in the denominator and receives zero. Also, a ten-path answer cannot completely recover a task with more than ten required files; two tasks in this cohort cross that bound.

Read a little farther

One guess, five guesses, ten guesses. Replay reveals the actual scores at those three cutoffs. The vertical scale is the same in each panel: how many of the 85 issues were recovered?

How much does a larger answer recover?

Same 85 issues in every panel · actual cutoffs 1, 5 and 10

Qwen’s any-file recovery rises from 35 issues at rank one to 73 at ten. Jev with structural context raises those counts to 52 and 78. Complete recovery at ten is lower: 38 for Qwen, 47 for the structural condition. The extra search depth and the judgment step answer different parts of the problem.

The same issues, side by side

An aggregate gain does not mean every issue improves. Each thin column below follows one historical issue through all six procedures. Green means every required file was found; amber means only part of the fix; muted pink means none. The marks retain the repository grouping so repeated issues from one codebase remain visible.

510 outcomes, one column per issue

Six rows = procedures · 85 columns = issues · 22 repository groups

The exact scores

The default table gives every eligible task equal weight. “Repositories equally” first averages within each repository, then averages the 22 repository means. The plots above use the 85-task view; changing the table’s scope does not change their denominator.

Nine procedures, the same historical labels

Exact canonical metrics · Complete means FileAcc · percentages and task counts

The table includes three extra structural procedures. The main plots compare six procedures; archived CodeRankEmbed and replicated results remain in the downloadable source tables. There is no 85-task BM25 result to publish.

On all 85 tasks, QS reaches 78 any-file hits and 47 complete recoveries. Inspected Sol reaches 65 and 41. On the final slice of 15 tasks, QS has 14 any-file hits and inspected Sol has 13; both completely recover ten. Four repository groups are too few for a broad generalization.

A difference in these totals does not, by itself, isolate the value of model size, Atlas, or any particular relationship. The procedures have different inputs and output behavior.

What does Atlas do without embeddings?

Start with words in the issue, and use no model calls. P matches those words against paths. P+A also recognizes named files or functions—starting clues called anchors. P+A+F adds direct connections. P+A+D also uses Theory’s saved relationship answers.

Structure without a model

Four deterministic procedures · 85 tasks · source preparation still costs time

At ten files, the path-only method finds something in 30/85 issues. Named starting points raise that to 35/85, a net gain of five issues. The full structural method also finds 35/85, and recovers every required file in 18/85, compared with 14/85 for paths alone. At rank one, anchors raise hits from 10 to 16; adding the later structural scores reduces that count. Structure is useful here, but more structural scoring is not automatically better.

This is structure without models, not without a starting clue. Preparing the source facts still costs time.

The architecture census helps explain why a repository can have rich, recognizable structure without an equally strong localization signal. Common utilities serve many behaviors, public entry points hide implementation files, and dynamic dependencies can escape the recorded relationships. These are source-grounded explanations to investigate, not a causal test proving why the aggregate gain is small.

Path-word matching: the baseline you can calculate yourself

Could we do this with word matching alone? P compares the issue with each file’s path—its filename and folders. It never reads the implementation. Try this small example:

Try path-word matching by hand

P · exact tokenizer and tie rule · five instructional paths

Lowercase, split into word-like pieces, discard pieces shorter than three characters, and remove repeats. Count the whole words shared with the issue. Put larger counts first; break ties by the original path. These pieces are called tokens, but they are not model billing tokens.

The small trap: receipt_total stays one word, and receiptTotal becomes receipttotal. Neither splits into receipt and total. A separator is anything except a letter, digit or underscore.

pathTokens is the path’s word list. foldLeft starts at zero and visits the issue words: add one if the word is present, otherwise keep the count. The score is a count, not a probability. There is no stemming, semantic similarity, learned weight or hidden inference call.

Read the exact tokenizer

The code uses Char.isLetterOrDigit, including Unicode letters; the old ASCII-only comment is narrower than the implementation. c :: rest separates the next character from the rest of the list; Nil ends it. Accepted characters extend current. A separator finishes that piece and starts another. The final filter keeps pieces of length at least three, and distinct removes repeats. The ordering key reverses score order and then uses the path to break ties.

P misses behavior whose name is absent from the path. Qwen also sees source text. P and Q are alternative starting rankings, not two steps in sequence. Beating P means beating this simple rule, not every possible word-search method.

BM25: a measured comparison on one issue

BM25 searches for the issue’s words in file paths and source text. Matching a term that appears in few files contributes more; term frequency and document length also affect the score. The retained Greenwood recording compares BM25 and Qwen on exactly the same 393 candidate paths. This is an existing recording, not a new model run.

BM25 and Qwen on the same eight fixing files

One recorded Greenwood issue · exact ranks among 393 candidates

Qwen puts five of the eight fixing files in the first ten; BM25 puts three there. But BM25 ranks the shared resource-utils.js helper at 11, ahead of Qwen’s 24. That counterexample is useful: the embedding improves several ranks without improving every rank. Neither method recovers the whole fix at ten in this recording.

BM25’s one-issue result is not P’s 30/85 cohort score. Different method, different evidence.

What did Sol actually do?

The frontier comparison uses gpt-6.1-sol at medium effort. The original and inspected runs are distinct frozen arms. The original run observed no tool calls and often abstained; treating it as a strong repository-reading baseline would be misleading. The inspected run explicitly required searching and reading implementation files before returning up to ten existing paths.

ProcedureHow it gets evidenceWhat it returns
Qwen → Atlas → JevSaved embeddings order the admitted candidates. Atlas context and Jev judgment concern the first 32.A complete ranking. We evaluate its first k files.
Sol · originalPublic issue and clean-world setup; no observed tool calls in these turns.Up to 10 paths; many abstentions. Mean 0.66 across 88 turns.
Sol · inspectedExplicit instruction to search and read implementation. 300-second, 32-round and 256,000-token bounds.Up to 10 paths, in its own order. Mean 3.23 across 88 turns. A read requirement gates acceptance.

Both Sol procedures were one bounded turn per task. They saw the public issue and clean repository, with the historical labels withheld. The inspected run returned a mean of 3.23 paths across 88 turns, rather than a complete candidate ranking. Its prompt asked it to avoid padding an answer. A ten-position scoring window is therefore not the same thing as ten returned predictions.

Each finds things the other misses

Inspected Sol finds a required file in all seven tasks that QS misses. QS has 20 hits that inspected Sol is scored as missing; 19 of those Sol results fail the recorded implementation-read requirement described below. Both hit 58 tasks. Switch to complete recovery and the overlap changes again. This is a comparison of existing answers, not a proposed ensemble or a newly evaluated combined system.

Which issues does each procedure recover?

One mark = one task · paired QS and inspected Sol outcomes

The Sol scores have an important qualification. The inspected procedure required a recorded nonempty implementation read. 20 of 88 turns fail that requirement; 19 are in the 85-task scoring cohort. Their receipts contain inspection commands, but the frozen projection could not name an implementation read. The original scoring keeps those tasks as misses. They are not 19 demonstrated failures to reason about the code.

The following Flix function shows exactly where that requirement enters. An otherwise successful turn with no qualifying read becomes a protocol failure before its paths reach the metric reducer. The website preserves that rule; it does not silently rescore the raw answer.

Open the actual answers

FxTS illustrates a real Sol success where QS misses the only eligible required file. Greenwood illustrates why a scored Sol miss can be an instrumentation issue: the raw answer names relevant files, but its inspection record fails the declared requirement. Carbon shows complete recovery by Sol where QS finds only part of the fix.

Two procedures, one historical issue

Saved predictions and evaluator labels · no new model call

The preparation bill is not just inference

The source reader recognizes definitions, imports and calls; Flix checks their targets. In the recorded build, the longest extraction process took 42.5 minutes. A fast judgment on prepared data does not erase that cost. Replay all 92 extraction actions and inspect their timing distribution.

What we learned—and what we did not

Learned retrieval is strong in this panel. Narrow judgment improves its ordering, and structural context adds a smaller aggregate improvement with individual regressions. Sol’s different procedure recovers issues that the ranked pipeline misses. None of these observations establishes general model superiority, causal credit for a particular Atlas operator, or performance on an unseen architectural population.

The benchmark labels are change-path labels, not a manually verified minimum explanation. New files, unsupported source and tests can matter to a real fix while being ineligible here. Source names and code snippets in an issue can make retrieval easier. These limits are part of the problem being measured, not footnotes to remove from the denominator.

architecture:
Follow a connection. What happens next?

Start at Greenwood’s resource-utils.js. It imports hashing-utils.js. Now ask who imports that file. Three files answer, including the one we started from.

One file. Nine different questions.

Greenwood w49 · eight nonempty answers · one empty branch

Each step takes the files we have, follows one relationship, and replaces the current set with the answer. That sequence is a route. Imports; ImportedBy reads “find imports; then find their importers.”

Files{...} lists exact files; Symbols{...} lists named pieces of code, such as functions. [OK] means the set has members. [EMPTY] means none. This current set is the frontier—where the next step starts, not everywhere we have been.

Eight of these nine questions return something. One returned item and 58 returned items each count as one answered question. “8/9 still find something” does not mean eight files found, or eight bugs solved.

The steps must fit together. Imports takes files; Calls takes named code items. Defines; Calls fits because Defines finds the names inside a file. Imports; Calls does not. This check is what typed means here.

Nothing in, nothing out

Ask what hashing-utils.js imports and the recorded answer is empty. There is no file left for the next step to start from.

Nothing in. Nothing out.

A dead branch stays empty · another branch may still find something

That is extinction: once this route empties out, continuing it cannot bring anything back. Asking a different question before the empty step can still find three consumers. Dead route, useful file.

Empty answers tell us where these particular connections run out. A short chain could explain one; a dynamic call the reader cannot resolve could explain another. They describe the accepted facts, not everything the program does.

We already answered this

One question starts with a function and finds its file. Another starts right at that file. Both now ask what the same file imports. Watch the second borrow the first answer:

Asked once. Used twice.

Checked shop example · follow the repeated question

Try changing B to checkout.rb. It imports the same pricing file, but the saved question starts at receipt.rb. The new question needs its own calculation. Same destination, different work.

The saved answer belongs to the question “what does this exact file set import?” We do not need to follow those connections twice. Saving a calculation’s answer for the same request is called memoization.

(typed input state, next operation)
    -> typed output state

Here “state” just means the files or named code items currently in hand. [OK; REUSE t4] tells two things: the answer has members, and computation t4 supplied it. An empty answer can be saved too. A failed calculation is different.

Prefix caching shares the beginning of two routes. Atlas can also share work after different beginnings, if they arrive at the same exact question. Matching output counts alone is not enough; two sets of ten files might have no members in common.

What must match? The actual key and lookup
(world, memo namespace, exact typed input, next atom)
    -> exact typed output

The world identifies the repository version and its interpretation rules. A memo namespace separates calculations that must not share answers. An atom is one relationship operation. All four parts must match:

Some((ordinal, output)) means a saved set was found; Hit(ordinal) points to the original computation. None means we must do the work. After successful apply, :: memo saves the new entry. Empty results count as successful answers; errors do not.

Two different questions can independently produce the same output. That does not retroactively share their work. Only if they then ask the same next question can that later computation be shared.

There are several different kinds of saved work. The Grit process memo keeps compiled patterns and file-extraction results under matching language, program, path and source; a process restart loses it. Atlas keeps exact relationship answers in a world-scoped memo. Bazel keeps declared action outputs. Inference fixtures keep vectors or decisions with their input/model/recipe identity. A retained fixture is not a provider-side cache hit.

Unchanged file extraction can survive a source edit, but repository resolution may still change elsewhere: a new definition can make a formerly unique name ambiguous. The transition memo cannot silently cross into the new world. Wall Time shows the measured reuse boundaries.

Does every repository answer the same way?

We tried the same family of questions on 78 saved versions of 11 repositories. Eight files and eight named code items start each version’s questions. Some paths run out quickly. Others keep returning answers.

What is ordinary in this sample?

Eleven repository profiles · the shaded band is the middle half

Read rightward for more steps; upward for more questions still returning something. The shaded band holds the middle half of eleven repository profiles. Each repository counts once, even when we have many versions of it. This is an ordinary range in this sample, not a model of all repositories.

That profile is a structural signature: how the same questions answer in different codebases. Across all route lengths, the middle repository has 63.18% empty file-start answers. The middle half lies between 52.44% and 75.25%.

Which questions, and what is the denominator?

Every starting point receives all type-correct routes of lengths one through seven: 3,279 routes, or 52,464 answers per version across sixteen starts. No issue or fix chooses them. Each next step has three legal options. Thus eight file starts produce 72 two-step answers and 17,496 seven-step answers.

For example, NodeBB c5ae8a70 has 23/72 = 31.94% nonempty two-step file answers. That percentage counts questions, not files reached or issues solved. The band first takes each repository’s median across versions, then the middle half of those eleven profiles. There are 22 NodeBB versions but only one Babel version. Individual curves and source identities.

Empty, broad, repeated

Three repositories can answer the same question very differently: nothing, a huge set, or something we already calculated. Those differences matter for both usefulness and work.

Three properties, eleven repositories

Empty answers · answer breadth · repeated work

Empty counts questions returning nothing. Broad measures the returned set as a share of its type’s population: 20 of 100 functions is 20%; 20 of 1,000 files is 2%. The graph uses the 90th percentile—nine tenths of answer sizes fall at or below it. Repeated work compares route counts with actual relationship evaluations. That multiplier counts avoided calculations, not seconds saved.

Immutable keeps answering

Immutable’s symbol-start questions stay nonempty more often than any other repository here: 57.47% across all lengths, and 57.30% at seven steps. Plenty still end empty.

Immutable: more symbol questions stay alive

Two retained versions · the same reference band and scales

One starting path is src/predicates/isList.js. A predicate is a function asking a yes/no question, but that filename does not explain this curve by itself. We would need to inspect the connections. Immutable is in this signature study, not the 85-issue localization cohort.

Babel runs out—and remembers that

99.48% of Babel’s file-start routes finish empty: only 137 of 26,232 return something. Here is the catch: all eight starting files are test fixtures, little programs used to test the compiler. They are not a tour of Babel’s implementation.

Babel: file questions mostly stop

One retained version · all eight file starts are test fixtures

Once many routes reach an empty set, they keep asking the same few questions of it. Those saved empty answers are reusable.

Many routes, very few distinct questions

Sixteen Babel starts · measured evaluations, not claimed speedups

For one numeric-separator fixture, 3,279 routes need only nine relationship evaluations. Their 21,324 step requests contain nine calculations and 21,315 reuses, producing two distinct output states. Very efficient. Mostly empty.

Babel’s function starts tell a different story, also shown above. At the other end, Element’s file routes stay nonempty 72.86% of the time; its 90th-percentile answer covers 70.62% of the relevant population. Lots of neighbors can mean useful shared code—or far too much context for one bug.

How much work was shared?

More questions than calculations

1,248 starting-point executions · every point is retained evidence

Each point is one of 1,248 recorded starting-point executions. They show measured work counts in the historical route study, not measured speedups. The shop example earlier demonstrates the current exact-key rule; these older recordings supply the larger comparison.

What are these connections for?

A curve cannot tell us whether a file is a plugin, a helper or a public entry point. For that, open the code. In the separate localization census, 28 deeply inspected issues yielded forty confirmed examples in twelve categories.

Choose a row to see the participating files and what they do. The small strips keep the same 22 repository positions, so repeated patterns line up.

Choose a pattern. Open its source.

12 linked patterns · 22 fixed repository positions · inspected evidence only

A blank means not established by this inspection, not “absent from the repository.” Naming a folder plugins was not enough to confirm a plugin architecture.

For a shared helper, we can first ask which two different files import the same target:

Both Imports lines share center; a != b excludes self-pairs. That establishes a shared dependency. Reading its implementation tells us what role it plays. Theory’s frozen 72-question family has no inequality and permits self-pairs; those questions are not the twelve human-confirmed design patterns. Atlas connects rules to actual saved rows.

Repetition has a local accent

People repeat coding choices. Naturalness research measures how predictable that makes source text. Localness asks where those repetitions occur: a project may repeat its own names and phrases more strongly than a general model expects. See Hindle and colleagues’ On the Naturalness of Software (2012) and Tu, Su and Devanbu’s On the Localness of Software (2014).

Here we ask a different question: does code repeat the same relationship answers? If so, we may reuse a calculation. These plots do not reproduce those papers’ text-prediction results or show that a signature predicts a fix.

Sharing more code can also connect more parts

“Local” can also mean dependencies staying within a group of files. An earlier AttuneFlix study compared two revisions with the same ten groups. Files increased from 72 to 75; imports crossing groups rose from 86.7% to 88.8%. For all 45 pairs of groups, at least half of their combined two-step neighborhoods were shared, before and after cleanup.

Removing duplicate implementation can increase shared dependencies. That is not automatically a design defect, but it can make a two-step neighborhood a blunt clue to a bug. These are the v2 Grit-based measurements for bcfc126d → ae2f5e68, not the earlier path-word proxy. Retained research notes · identities and hashes.

A repository can also keep a similar profile through many edits. Attune over time puts those edits beside the answers, including changes hidden by a steady headline.

Useful structure is not automatically a useful clue

A shared helper may serve many unrelated features. A public entry point may point toward the right area while hiding the file that needs changing. This census gives concrete reasons to investigate Atlas’s modest aggregate gain; it does not prove their causes.

In the localization experiment, Atlas supplies candidate notes to Jev—not this whole-repository signature, or new files beyond Qwen’s first 32. That adds one any-file success and two complete fixes over basic Jev. The resulting totals are 78/85 and 47/85. Without either model, the path-and-structure procedure scores 35/85 and 18/85, still starting from the issue’s words.

Different shapes, less repeated work, better file recovery: three separate questions. A useful result in one does not settle the others.

Same shape does not mean same code

Similar summary     != identical answers
Same answer size    != same answer members
Similar connections != unchanged behavior
Similar signature   != permission to reuse a cache

A small edit to a central connection can affect many answers. A large rewrite can preserve the connections we measure. These checkpoints show both persistence and change; they do not establish a universal rule relating edit size to structure.

Exact reuse asks a stricter question: are the repository world, input set and next operation identical? That is what Atlas checks before taking a saved answer.

It is not just the final answer’s size.

overview:
Different work. Different waits.

Understanding a codebase involves several kinds of work: reading source, asking models, following relationships, and checking answers. Attune makes those steps explicit so we can measure them, schedule independent work, and keep answers that are still valid.

Five kinds of wait

707 recorded operations · every dot is a measurement

The long tail matters. Source extraction took 93.77 seconds at the median, but 344.58 seconds on average; the slowest process took 42.5 minutes. A small prepared judgment and a whole repository-inspection turn have different costs—and different timer boundaries.

These distributions tell us where to investigate. They do not measure a scheduler’s speedup. Explore recorded overlap, cold acquisition, and warm replay →

Ask for work. Decide how to perform it.

A calculation can ask for an embedding without deciding whether to call a provider or use a saved answer. An effect makes that request visible; a handler supplies the answer and the calculation continues.

Ask. Answer. Carry on.

Compiled Flix teaching example · no live provider request

Flix checks the requests; Bazel schedules the actions. A saved answer applies only to the same input, model, and recipe. Follow the handoff, then run it yourself →

Change the question. Keep the unaffected work.

source files ──> facts ──> structural questions
       └──────> vectors ──> candidate files ──> judgment
                                    ↑
                              issue-specific input

Bazel declares which steps depend on which inputs. Unchanged artifacts can be reused; independent actions can run together through BuildBuddy. Follow cold acquisition, warm replay, and incremental reuse →

A separate historical AttuneFlix evaluation preserved outputs across 61 JS/TS cases: 4,301.12 seconds of sequential shard work became 51.70 seconds of cold remote wall time, and the warm graph took 0.153 seconds. This is offline evaluation and exact replay, not a live coding-agent speedup. Sealed measurements →

Qwen retrieval: 33× lower known model spend

Qwen’s recorded embedding acquisition cost $0.141, versus about $4.65 estimated for frontier-model repository inspection across 88 tasks. Adding structural context and Jev judgment cost $0.165—28× below that estimate.

Qwen found a required file within ten on 85.9% of 85 eligible issues, versus 76.5% for the inspection arm. Sol was stronger at the first file and complete recovery. These workflows give models different work. The dollar comparison excludes computer costs; Sol’s subscription bill is unknown.

Cold acquisition made 351 embedding requests; unchanged warm replay made zero. Warm wall time was not measured. Explore the cost comparison → · Follow reuse →

Does the extra structure help find the right files?

Localization asks which existing files an issue’s reference fix touches. The retained SWE-rebench-V2 comparison scored 85 eligible issues across 22 repository groups. Qwen orders candidates; Atlas adds structural context as post-processing; Jev judges the shortlist.

Follow recovery across the same issues

Frozen localization results · top-one, top-ten, and required-file recovery

Top-one accuracy was 41.2% for Qwen, 57.6% with Jev reranking, and 61.2% with structural context added to that prompt. Structure also made some fixes harder to recover. The final split contains only 15 eligible issues; this is exploratory evidence.

Watch one issue move through all three stages → · Inspect successes and regressions → · Read populations, costs, and comparison limits →

Can several agents work in one worktree?

Coordination uses the same code connections as localization to divide work between agents in one checkout. Separate work can run in parallel; overlapping changes need coordination. The rules pass tests on authored examples. The original 32-pair study is unfinished. Read the parallelism experiment →

What changes when the task is review?

Could saved knowledge of a repository make review cheaper? ReviewBench tested that idea. A reviewer already starts with a code change and must find real defects and explain them; finding files became a smaller part of the job.

In the corrected check of 24 reserved tasks, ordinary access produced 18 valid findings, versus 17 with optional packets, counting final reviews and saved checkpoints. Across the pilot and later check, the packet tool refused all three calls. The setup did not show a cost-saving benefit. Results, corrections, and resource accounting →

Small programs you can inspect

Files define functions, files import files, and functions call functions. Attune turns those relationships into typed questions with exact answer sets and source witnesses. In localization, that structure supplies context for judging a retrieved shortlist.
